title: Say it out loud (1:1)
hook: return includes spoken confession: I did this, I regret it, I won't again
tomorrow: you said sorry. how would you ever know you've really changed?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new book: Maimonides' ten chapters on returning, and a first law that opens the mouth. Today, what the mouth says.
screen: `TEN CHAPTERS ON RETURNING.` → `WHAT THE MOUTH SAYS.`

segments.voice: You type sorry. You delete it. You type sorry about the other day. Delete. You feel it, honestly, all the way down. So isn't feeling sorry enough? Maimonides' answer is short: no. Feeling is where it starts, but the return isn't finished inside your chest. It has to come out as words. In Hebrew that spoken confession has a name: vidui.
screen: `SORRY. DELETE.` → `ISN'T FEELING ENOUGH?` → `IT HAS TO BE SAID.`

segments.voice: The question: what does real return need? Here is Maimonides' answer, in plain words. The confession goes like this: please, God, I have sinned, I have done wrong before You, and I did this, naming it. And I regret it, and I'm ashamed of what I did, and I will never go back to this. He calls that the heart of vidui, and says whoever says more is praised. Three moves: I did this. I regret it. I won't again. And notice the middle of the first one: naming it. Not sorry for everything. This. Now a neighbor. In Islam, the scholar al-Nawawi, in his collection Riyad as-Salihin, teaches that turning back to God, tawbah, has conditions: stop the wrong, regret it, and resolve never to return to it. And if the wrong was against a person, make it right with them. Shared ground: the same three moves, almost word for word. Stop, regret, resolve. Two traditions that honor many of the same prophets also share a map of coming home. And an honest difference. Nawawi's conditions live in the heart and the deed, between the person and God. Maimonides adds that the return must also be said out loud, the deed named in words. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: on Yom Kippur, the community says a long vidui together, in the plural, ashamnu, we have been guilty, so nobody has to stand up and say it alone.
screen: `WHAT DOES RETURN NEED?` · `I DID THIS. I REGRET. NOT AGAIN.` · `A NEIGHBOR: STOP, REGRET, RESOLVE.` · `MAIMONIDES ADDS: SAY IT.` · then, large: `SAY IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Find a quiet spot and choose one small thing to come back from. Following Maimonides' outline, say three short sentences softly out loud: I did this, naming it. I regret it. I won't again. Then sit in the quiet the words leave behind.
screen: `ONE SMALL THING.` · `I DID THIS. I REGRET IT. NOT AGAIN.` · `SIT IN THE QUIET.`

segments.voice: Vidui. Spoken confession: the deed named out loud, with regret and a resolve not to return to it.
Your line: say it out loud, and name the thing. Two of thirty in the laws of return.

screen: `DAY 1539 COUNTS.` → `THE LAWS OF RETURN · 2 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: YOU SAID SORRY. HOW WOULD YOU EVER KNOW YOU'VE REALLY CHANGED?`

howItsDone: Vidui is said in the Yom Kippur prayers, many times, and in some communities in daily prayers; Maimonides' own short formula is a model for private confession before God.

fork.setup: your brother broke your headphones and says, 'my bad, whatever happened, sorry.' what's missing, by Maimonides' outline?
options: naming it: I broke your headphones, I regret it, I won't again.
nothing: any sorry counts as long as he means it inside.
a gift: words never count without something to make up for it.
fork.reveal: vidui names the deed, says the regret, and resolves not to return. 'whatever happened' skips the first step.

original.note: Hebrew: confession, spoken aloud. Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a guilty feeling you keep to yourself.
what it means: in Maimonides' law, the one returning speaks straight to God, naming the deed, the regret and the resolve.
what a scholar hears: Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1 gives the formula and calls it the essence of confession, praising one who adds; the Yom Kippur vidui (Ashamnu, Al Chet) is said in the plural.

chat.says: going to apologize to mom tonight. do i say what i actually said, or just 'sorry about the other day'?
options: Name it. Maimonides wants the deed in words: I said this, I regret it, not again.
Keep it vague. Repeating what you said will only hurt her all over again.
Skip the words. Make her breakfast; actions always say it better than talk.
chat.meaning: Maimonides' vidui names the deed out loud, then the regret, then the resolve. 'Sorry about the other day' skips the naming.

vidui.meaning: spoken confession: naming a wrong out loud

al-Nawawi.meaning: a medieval Muslim scholar who compiled Riyad as-Salihin

tawbah.meaning: Arabic: turning back to God; repentance in Islam

ashamnu.meaning: we have been guilty: the Yom Kippur confession, said together
